title: Intrinsic optical signal imaging and targeted injections through a chronic cranial window of a head-fixed mouse
protocol: Weigh the animal.
Induce anesthesia with 3% isoflurane in an O2 induction chamber.
Transfer the mouse into its cage for 5 minutes to transition smoothly to deep anesthesia.
Inject a mixture of Medetomidine, Midazolam, and Butorphanol intraperitoneally before isoflurane wears off.
Head-fix the mouse on the imaging stage using the headplate.
Position the brain surface perpendicular to the axis of the objective lens.
Cover the eyes with a drop of silicone or mineral oil to protect the cornea from drying.
Turn on the heating pad after inserting the rectal temperature sensor.
Maintain body temperature between 35°C and 37°C throughout the procedure.
Apply 0.25%–1% isoflurane anesthesia in O₂ and maintain it throughout the imaging session.
Clean the window with small cotton-tips moistened with water.
Optimize the window illumination with the white / green LED by adjusting the gooseneck light guide.
Focus with the camera on the brain surface using a low-magnification lens.
Adjust the camera settings to center the region of interest.
If applicable, adjust the active sensor size so that no unnecessary data is acquired.
Take the reference image of the brain surface vasculature.
Use the green light illumination or green light pass filter for high-contrast images.
Focus 400–600 μm below the brain surface.
Lowering the focal plane to minimize the intrinsic signal mediated by the large vasculature on the brain surface.
Turn off the white / green LED light source.
Remove the green filter from the light path if used.
Optimize cortical illumination with the high-power red (615–655 nm) LED light source using the gooseneck light guide.
Wear red-light filter goggles when looking at the illuminated setup.
Ensure the high-power LED light is not directed into the eyes of the mouse or experimenter.
Make sure that the light is not reflected from the window glass surface into the objective lens.
Adjust camera settings for highest signal-to-noise ratio.
Record frames at 100–195 Hz with a sCMOS camera (PCO.edge, PCO).
Use an exposure time of 5 ms.
Capture 1200×950 px frames in full dynamic range 16-bit format (.tiff).
Adjust the power of the LED light source to use the full dynamic range without saturation.
Set the camera exposure time to 5 ms for optimal imaging conditions.
Keep the image position and number of pixels consistent with previous settings for alignment purposes.
Record 5–6 imaging trials, each consisting of a 1 s black screen, followed by 1 s visual stimulation, and then another 3 s black screen.
Include a 1–2 min waiting period with a black screen before each trial begins.
Ensure at least 10-s inter-trial intervals for visual stimulations lasting up to 2 seconds.
Synchronize the image acquisition and stimulus sequence presentation using an oscilloscope.
Process the recorded stacks of images using FIJI plugin “IO and VSD signal processor”.
Filter the images with 20 pixel sigma Gaussian in x and y, and ± 10 voxel average in z.
Calculate the average ratio image to show stimulation induced changes in red light reflectance.
Determine the difference between the averages of baseline frames (recorded 1s before stimulus onset) and response frames (frames recorded for 1–2s with <0.5 s delay after stimulus onset).
Record additional trials after switching from visual stimulation to somatosensory stimulation.
Deliver air-puff to the whisker pad during imaging trials.
Process V1 and BF trials separately.
Overlay images of averaged responses during offline data processing for mapping HVAs and posterior parietal cortex.
Inject Atipamezole hydrochloride (0.3 μL / g, ip; dissolved in 0.9% saline) for faster waking.
Repeat data processing to generate a clear image of V1.
Allow additional days for recovery if the intrinsic signal map is not revealed.
Encircle the functional response, defining V1, on the signal image with the ROI Manager plugin of FIJI.
Adjust the signal image to a threshold for the color map.
Choose the threshold as half of the intensity value of the peak in the smoothed intensity histogram of the signal ROI.
Anesthetize and head-fix the mouse using 3% isoflurane in an anesthesia induction chamber.
Maintain anesthesia throughout the procedure using 0.5%-1% isoflurane.
Head-fix the mouse on the imaging stage using the headplate.
Connect the microinjection pipette to the manometer.
Mount the microinjection pipette on the micromanipulator.
Position the beveled side of the pipette-tip sideways or upwards.
Measure the mounting angle of the pipette and micromanipulator settings for the angle of the diagonal movement direction.
Set the angles to be the same as specified in step 26e.
Check the trajectory of the pipette.
Define the central point of your injection target on the surface of the cranial window.
Move the pipette to that point.
Zero the coordinates.
Calculate the injection depth d = a + b + c.
Use a cortical depth (a) of 950 μm for layer 6 in the mouse primary visual cortex.
Use a cranial window glass thickness (b) of 170 μm.
Choose a distance above the glass (c) of 380 μm.
Lift the pipette by the distance c and reset coordinates to zero.
Switch to diagonal movement mode.
Retract the pipette so it lifts by distance d.
Switch back to regular, orthogonal movement mode.
Lower the pipette by distance d to reach the zero point.
Switch to the diagonal movement mode and approach the surface of the access port.
Slowly move forward until the pipette tip penetrates the silicone.
If the pipette bends or slides on the port’s surface, lift the pipette and repeat the procedure.
If the pipette might hit the glass, lift the pipette and repeat the procedure.
If a big superficial blood vessel is encountered, lift the pipette and repeat the procedure.
Change the mounting/diagonal movement angle if necessary.
Reconsider the target injection site if necessary.
Tip-fill the pipette with the viral vector containing solution.
Free some space over the headplate by moving the pipette to the side.
Place a small (5×10 mm) piece of parafilm with a 2 μL droplet of AAV solution on the headplate.
Bring back the pipette to the headplate and apply weak positive pressure (10–14 hPa).
Lower the pipette tip into the droplet under visual guidance.
Tip-fill the pipette with up to 300 nL of solution using negative pressure (typically −150 to −200 hPa).
Judge the volume by the tick marks on the pipette (in a 0.3 mm inner diameter pipette, 1 mm corresponds to a volume of 70 nL).
Replace the pipette in case of clogging.
Try a larger tip diameter pipette and/or additional dilution with PBS if necessary.
Apply weak positive pressure (10–14 hPa) and lift the pipette up.
Maintain this pressure until the injection of the solution into the brain.
Wipe the pipette tip with a PBS-soaked sterile sponge.
Lower the pipette into the brain aiming at the target injection site (z5 in Figure 5A).
Move the pipette to the center of your target area and zero the coordinates when the tip of the pipette touches the glass surface (z1 in Figures 5A and 6C).
Select the injection target region in V1, ensuring it is devoid of large blood vessels above the future imaging area.
Position the pipette tip at the glass surface of the cranial window directly above the target site.
Move the pipette to the silicone surface of the access port.
Fill the pipette tip with a drop of the viral vector solution.
Observe the injection speed and volume during delivery.
Insert the pipette into the brain with the tip at the estimated target site for injection.
Lift the pipette by the distance c and zero the coordinates again.
Switch to the diagonal movement mode and retract/lift the pipette by the distance d.
Switch back to the orthogonal movement mode and lower the pipette by the distance d to the zero point.
Switch to the diagonal movement mode and insert the pipette into the brain, moving down/forward by the distance d.
Focus on the access port.
Observe the penetration of the silicone, dura, and motion of the pipette till the injection site is reached.
Consider using a more rigid or sharper tip if necessary to penetrate the dura.
Reevaluate the angle and injection site if encountering a blood vessel or risk of breaking the pipette.
Wait for 3–5 minutes before initiating the injection process.
Visualize the meniscus in the pipette under observation.
Inject approximately 70-100 nL of solution using pressure (typically 35–70 hPa) within 5-7 minutes.
Reduce positive pressure to an initial level of 10-14 hPa and wait for 10 minutes to allow the injected solution to spread locally.
Retract the pipette slowly and smoothly.
Observe that the silicone of the access port seals immediately after pipette retraction.
